updated: 3 Sep 2026, 22:46 UTC — JMA active-cyclone feed + port/terminal advisories
sources: JMA bosai typhoon feed (targetTc.json + specifications.json), read 3 Sep 2026 22:46 UTC (4 Sep JST). Two systems still active. TC2628 Krovanh, storm No. 2624, category TS, issue 4 Sep 06:45 JST: analysis position 29.3N 128.1E southwest of Kyushu, forecast to drift southwest to 28.4N 127.1E at +24h and 26.0N 127.1E at +45h before recurving east and decaying to a TD by +117h. Closest approach to a tracked port is Shanghai/Ningbo at 564 km on the +24h forecast point; Busan is nearest at 651 km, outside the 600 km threshold, so Busan is not scored as a threat this run. TC2621 Saudel, storm No. 2618, has been downgraded from TS to TD, issue 3 Sep 22:05 JST, single analysis position 24.0N 116.0E over inland eastern Guangdong after its third landfall. It sits 217 km from Xiamen and 266 km from Shenzhen but is dissipating.

SEKO Asia-Pacific Logistics Monitoring Center, Week 36 update, last revised Thursday 3 September 2026 12:00 HKT — one day fresher than the revision available on the previous run. Headline status: Saudel made third landfall at Gulei, Zhangpu County, Zhangzhou (Fujian) at about 06:30 HKT on 3 September with Force 9 sustained winds and 985 hPa, and no new operational impacts or terminal closures have occurred at Ningbo, Shanghai or Xiamen. Terminal-level detail: Shanghai (Yangshan and Waigaoqiao) 100% open, mainline berth waiting 6 to 9 days, Yangshan yard occupancy 84-86% and Waigaoqiao 76%; Ningbo-Zhoushan (Meishan, Beilun, Daxie, Chuanshan) fully operational with mainline berth waiting averaging 7 to 10 days and Meishan yard at 93-95%; Xiamen container terminals (Songyu, Hairun, Haicang) running normal vessel and gate operations with only passenger and Kinmen ferry routes suspended; Yantian operating under normal conditions with outer-anchorage swell subsided and mainline waiting 4 to 5 days under standard ETB-7 intake; Qingdao 1.5 to 2 days; Busan 1 to 2 days; Singapore 1 to 1.5 days.

The Loadstar and Sourcing Journal coverage of the post-Saudel queue, corroborating the SEKO figures and the direction of travel: berthing delays that peaked around 10 days at Shanghai and Ningbo immediately after the storm are now reported as elevated but stable and easing at Shanghai.

MSC customer advisories index, read 3 Sep 2026 22:46 UTC via Chrome: no port-closure or terminal-suspension notice for any Chinese or North Asian gateway. The most recent China-facing items are the 2026 Golden Week sailing programmes dated 24 and 26 August. This is corroborating negative evidence that no closure is currently in force.

Shanghai/Ningbo.waitLabel: Shanghai mainline berth waiting 6-9 days with Yangshan yard occupancy 84-86%; Ningbo-Zhoushan averaging 7-10 days with Meishan yard at 93-95% (SEKO, 3 Sep 12:00 HKT)
Shanghai/Ningbo.note: Terminals are open and have been since 28 August; what remains is queue, not closure. The Shanghai figure has come down from 7-10 days last run to 6-9, and the Loadstar peak of 10 days is now the top of the Ningbo range rather than the norm at both ports, so the direction is right even though the absolute numbers are still bad. Meishan yard occupancy at 93-95% is the constraint worth watching — that is where a second bunching event would bite first. The primary event name stays on Krovanh because Krovanh is the system currently nearest the Yangtze delta (564 km at +24h) while Saudel has crossed inland and been downgraded to a depression; the backlog itself is still Saudel-era. Krovanh is forecast to turn south and decay, so this entry will likely need its eventEnded set on the next run once the JMA feed drops it.
Shanghai/Ningbo.source: SEKO Asia-Pacific Logistics Monitoring Center Week 36 update, 3 Sep 2026 12:00 HKT; corroborated by The Loadstar and Sourcing Journal.

Xiamen.note: Watch is over. Saudel made its third landfall 06:30 HKT on 3 September at Zhangpu, roughly 90 km southwest of Xiamen, and is now a dissipating tropical depression inland. Container operations at Songyu, Hairun and Haicang were never interrupted — the only suspensions were passenger and Kinmen ferry services, which are not container operations and do not belong in a congestion picture. No source states a berth waiting time for Xiamen, so none is recorded. eventEnded is set to today (3 Sep UTC) so the entry tapers off rather than lingering.
Xiamen.source: SEKO Asia-Pacific Logistics Monitoring Center Week 36 update, 3 Sep 2026 12:00 HKT.

Shenzhen (Yantian).waitLabel: Mainline vessel waiting 4-5 days under standard ETB-7 export intake windows (SEKO, 3 Sep 12:00 HKT)
Shenzhen (Yantian).note: Watch is over. SEKO now describes Yantian as operating under normal conditions with outer-anchorage swell subsided as Saudel tracked inland, and the reported wait has eased from 5-6 days last run to 4-5. Linerlytica has Shenzhen at a queue-to-berth ratio of 0.385 on the 30 August snapshot, which is not a congested port by any reading. eventEnded is set to today (3 Sep UTC) so the entry tapers off rather than lingering.
Shenzhen (Yantian).source: SEKO Asia-Pacific Logistics Monitoring Center Week 36 update, 3 Sep 2026 12:00 HKT.

remarks: Linerlytica has not published a congestion snapshot since 30 August. The public window today runs 16-30 August and every one of those dates is already stored, so congestion.json was left untouched rather than restamped with a fresh date it does not deserve. Anything the congestion panel shows is five days old.
No port closures anywhere in the tracked set. Saudel is inland and decaying, Krovanh is forecast to turn south and weaken, and MSC has issued no closure advisory.
The story at Shanghai and Ningbo is now backlog rather than weather. Waits are easing at Shanghai (6-9 days, down from 7-10) but Ningbo is still 7-10 days with Meishan yard at 93-95%.
Xiamen and Shenzhen (Yantian) are both being retired from the panel: the systems that put them on watch have passed and neither ever stopped handling containers.
Everything outside the Saudel/Krovanh footprint is quiet — Qingdao 1.5-2 days, Busan 1-2 days, Singapore 1-1.5 days.
